description: Students from KNUST, Kumasi, Ghana. We build full-stack data tools and bring a systems mindset to scientific data problems. We honor the blink comparator, the instrument that revealed Pluto by flipping between sky images until something moved. We’re building its modern, automated version for NASA’s SPHEREx mission.
summary:
Blink is a public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx images into time-lapses. Enter sky coordinates, or pick a preset target, and Blink gathers every SPHEREx image of that patch from NASA’s IRSA archive, aligns them, sorts them by date and plays them like a short video. Moving and changing objects stand out against the fixed stars.

It addresses the “Planet X and SPHEREx” challenge directly: coordinate entry, a video-like series of images, a difference mode that subtracts the first frame so movers pop, co-adding of repeat visits to reveal faint objects, metadata with quality flags, and shareable links that restore any search. We tested it on Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

It matters because SPHEREx data sits in an archive that few people can explore. Blink lets students, educators and researchers see the sky change in seconds, and gives a simple first step toward spotting unknown moving objects.

At submission, IRSA’s SPHEREx search is down, so only the five cached targets return frames; live search resumes when it returns.
details:
Blink: watch the infrared sky move

What it does

Blink is a public web tool for NASA's SPHEREx mission. You enter sky coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) or pick one of five preset targets. Blink finds every SPHEREx image of that patch of sky in NASA's IRSA archive, lines them up, sorts them by date and plays them like a short video. Anything that moves or changes brightness stands out against the fixed background stars.

How it works

  • Fetch: a Python service queries IRSA's SPHEREx archive for every cutout covering the position in the chosen detector band, and downloads them.
  • Align: each image is reprojected onto the earliest one using its sky coordinates, so stars stay still between frames. Background is subtracted and all frames share one brightness scale, so the time-lapse doesn't flicker.
  • Play: the viewer steps through the frames with play/pause, speed control and a date scrubber. A red cross-hair marks the searched position.
  • Difference mode: each frame minus the first. Unchanged sky turns grey; a mover shows as a dark spot where it was and a bright spot where it went.
  • Co-add: SPHEREx images a patch several times within hours, then returns months later. Blink can average the frames of each visit into one, which cuts the noise and reveals faint targets such as WISE 0855.
  • Metadata: each frame shows its date, wavelength, band, frequency, detector, data release and quality flags.
  • Shareable links: the search lives in the URL, so a link reopens the same view and the tool can be embedded elsewhere.
  • Cache: results are cached, so a search that has run once loads instantly, even when the archive is unreachable. The five challenge targets ship pre-cached.

Current status of live search

At the time of submission (15 November 2026), the SPHEREx search service at NASA's IRSA archive is not responding, so Blink cannot fetch images for new coordinates. The five challenge targets still work, because their images were fetched earlier and are cached on our server. For any other position, Blink shows a clear message that the archive can't be reached. Live search should work again, with no change to Blink, once IRSA's service is back.

Benefits

  • Turns scattered archive files into something anyone can read in seconds, with no astronomy software.
  • Makes motion visible that is hard to see in single images: Barnard's Star shifts by nearly two SPHEREx pixels across thirteen months of frames.
  • Uses the newest data whenever the archive is reachable, because it queries it live.
  • Honest about the data: it shows the flags and notes that each visit is at a slightly different wavelength, so some brightness changes are colour, not motion.

Intended impact

We want students, educators and amateur astronomers to explore real mission data for themselves, and researchers to have a quick first look at any position before a deeper analysis. Because the same method works at any coordinates, it is also a simple starting point for spotting unknown moving objects, which is the spirit of the "Planet X" challenge.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA SPHEREx images from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), via its TAP and cutout services.
  • Image processing: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow.
  • API: Node.js, NestJS, Prisma, SQLite.
  • Website: React, TypeScript, Vite, three.js, Motion.
  • Hosting: Vercel (site), Render (API and image service), Docker.
  • Hardware: our own laptops; no special equipment.
  • AI assistance: we used an AI coding assistant (Claude) to help integrate and test the code.

How it is creative

  • It revives the blink comparator, the instrument Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto, as a web tool for a modern infrared survey.
  • It uses SPHEREx's own observing pattern, repeated visits within hours, to co-add frames and pull faint objects out of the noise.
  • The landing page shows a three.js sky sphere with a sweeping scan band that echoes how SPHEREx surveys the sky.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: target positions are moved to the SPHEREx epoch using proper motion, so fast movers sit in the frame.
  • Clarity for non-experts: SPHEREx pixels are large (about 6 arcseconds), so images are stretched, cleaned of flagged pixels and smoothly enlarged to be readable.
  • Reliability: the archive can be slow or unavailable, so results are cached and failures give a clear message instead of a crash.
  • Accessibility: readable contrast, keyboard focus, reduced-motion support and a layout that works on phones.
  • Safety of a public service: rate limiting, input validation and a cap on simultaneous new searches.
  • Known limits: IRSA's SPHEREx search is down at the time of submission, so only the five cached targets return frames; frames within one detector span a range of wavelengths; WISE 0855 is near the detection limit even after co-adding.

Tested on: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

Team SpaceWars: Christabel, Albert, Kwaku, Jude.

Credit: Data from NASA SPHEREx via IRSA/IPAC. Built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
